::: {.why}
The correction is arithmetic; the input is a confession, and the gap between what you logged and what you remember is the most useful number of the phase.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- State the difference between the trials you logged and the trials you would have reported from memory, and say which is closer to the truth.
- Describe the specific ways an adaptive search inflates the effective trial count beyond what a grid would give.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>55 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Audit yourself: read research_log.jsonl, count runs by strategy family, and compare against your day 49 guess. Then write down the trials that are not in the log at all, the ones you ran interactively and abandoned, and estimate how many there were.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Read the Harvey, Liu and Zhu paper's introduction and its argument about the effective number of tests in the published factor literature, and note the threshold t-statistic they end up recommending. Then say what the equivalent threshold is for your own work at your own trial count.
:::
:::

## Resources

- [Harvey, Liu & Zhu (2014) — ...and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns](https://www.nber.org/papers/w20592) [paper]{.res-kind}
- [McLean & Pontiff (draft) — Does Academic Research Destroy Stock Return Predictability?](https://www.hec.ca/finance/Fichier/McLean.pdf) [paper]{.res-kind}

## Deliverable

::: {.deliverable}
A trial-count audit in reports/milestone-02-noise-floor.md: logged, unlogged, estimated total, and the threshold each implies.
:::

## Checkpoint

::: {.checkpoint}
How many hypotheses have you actually tested since day 1, and how confident are you in that number to within a factor of two?
:::
